course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Chemical Reactions
unit.blurb: Physical and chemical changes, word equations and particle models, useful and harmful reactions, and the evidence that a reaction has happened.

O1.t: Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes.

O2.t: Write word equations, identify reactants and products, and use particle models to explain conservation of mass.

O3.t: Describe useful and harmful chemical reactions, including combustion, acid rain and rusting, and how rusting is prevented.

O4.t: Use evidence (colour change, precipitate, gas, reactants used up) and gas tests to decide whether a reaction has happened.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 9: Chemical Reactions.

Every farmer wants healthy crops, and most use fertilisers made by chemical reactions in giant factories. Chemical reactions are everywhere: in cooking, in our bodies, and in the air around us. Let's discover how they work, which help us, and which harm us.

Matter can change in two important ways. In a physical change, energy, transferred by heat, light or electricity, changes the shape or state of matter. Melting ice and tearing paper are physical changes: no new substance is made.
In a chemical change, also called a chemical reaction, substances react to form new substances. A burning candle and a rusting padlock are chemical changes.

Physical changes, like freezing and melting, are often easy to reverse. Chemical changes usually aren't: once wood burns to smoke and ash, it can't become wood again. A few reactions can be reversed, like the reaction inside a rechargeable battery when you recharge it.
Let's practise. Sugar dissolving in hot tea, bread being toasted, an iceberg melting, and mould growing on bread. Which are physical changes, and which are chemical?
Sugar dissolving and an iceberg melting are physical changes. The sugar and the water are still the same substances.
Toasting bread and mould growing are chemical changes. New substances form: the brown crust of toast, and the products made as mould feeds on the bread.
The key question is: has a new substance been made? If yes, it's a chemical change.

q.prompt: In acid + zinc → zinc chloride + hydrogen, the products are…

stops.note: Paused after: “A chemical reaction only rearranges atoms. It can't create or destroy them, or change them”

captions: We describe a reaction using a word equation. The starting substances, the reactants, go on the left. The new substances, the products, go on the right. The arrow shows the direction of the reaction.
For example, when carbon burns: carbon plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide.
And you met this one in Unit 8: acid plus alkali gives salt plus water.

Let's try one. Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to zinc, producing zinc chloride and hydrogen gas. The reactants, hydrochloric acid and zinc, go on the left; the products, zinc chloride and hydrogen, go on the right.
We can use particle models to see what happens in a reaction. Here's one carbon atom and one oxygen molecule, made of two oxygen atoms joined together.
Energy, such as heat, is needed to start the reaction. It breaks the oxygen molecule apart into separate atoms.
The carbon atom then joins with both oxygen atoms, forming one molecule of carbon dioxide.
So in every reaction, energy breaks the reactants apart, and the atoms rearrange to make new products. Sometimes even the warmth of the surroundings is enough to start a reaction.
Now hydrogen reacts with oxygen. Two hydrogen molecules and one oxygen molecule. Let's count the atoms: 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms.
Each oxygen atom joins two hydrogen atoms, making two water molecules. Count again: still 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms!
A chemical reaction only rearranges atoms. It can't create or destroy them, or change them into other elements. So the total mass stays the same. We call this the conservation of mass.

sections.title: Useful and harmful reactions

stops.note: Paused after: “Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen to make ammonia, the building block of most fer”
Paused after: “Acid rain also reacts with minerals in the soil and can kill whole forests. To protect the”
Paused after: “Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin protective oxide layer on the surfac”

captions: Many reactions are very useful. Burning, or combustion, of fuels like petrol releases a lot of energy to power vehicles. Carbon-containing fuel plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water.
Combustion and breathing use up oxygen, but photosynthesis in plants restores it. Using light, plants turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
Plastics are made by heating substances refined from crude oil and plants. They are light, cheap and easy to shape, but plastic waste can harm the environment.

Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen to make ammonia, the building block of most fertilisers, which help farmers grow enough food. Cooking, digestion and respiration in our bodies are useful reactions too.

Some reactions are harmful. Burning fuels makes greenhouse gases and pollutants that cause acid rain. Marble and limestone statues are made of calcium carbonate. Acid rain reacts with it, forming calcium sulfate, carbon dioxide and water, so the stone slowly corrodes.
Chalk cliffs, eggshells, and many shells and corals are calcium carbonate too, so they are also damaged by acids.
Acid rain also reacts with minerals in the soil and can kill whole forests. To protect them, foresters spread crushed limestone, which neutralises the acid.
Rusting is another harmful reaction. Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron oxide, or rust. Rust is flaky and much weaker than iron, so iron bridges must be checked for rust damage.
Luckily, we can prevent rusting. Painting steel gives it a protective layer that keeps out air and water.

Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin protective oxide layer on the surface. And iron objects, like watering cans, can be coated with zinc: the zinc corrodes instead of the iron underneath.

q.prompt: When magnesium 'disappears' in acid, its atoms…

captions: How can we tell that a chemical reaction has happened? New substances form, and we may see some clear signs. The first is a change in colour.
Second, a precipitate may form: a solid that appears in a solution.
Third, a gas may be given off, and we see bubbles. This is called effervescence.
And fourth, the reactants may seem to disappear. For example, mixing colourless sulfuric acid with white sugar produces black carbon. The colour change tells us a reaction has happened.

Place an iron nail in blue copper sulfate solution and wait an hour. The solution turns pale green, and a reddish layer of copper coats the nail. Iron plus copper sulfate gives iron sulfate plus copper.
Now mix two clear solutions: silver nitrate and sodium chloride. A white solid appears! Silver chloride is insoluble, so it separates out as a precipitate.
Each common gas has its own test. Add magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid, and it fizzes, making hydrogen. Hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube: a squeaky pop means hydrogen.
React vinegar with baking soda, and carbon dioxide is given off. Bubble it through limewater: the limewater turns milky as a white precipitate of calcium carbonate forms.
For oxygen, light a wooden splint, then blow it out so it's just glowing. Put it into the gas...
...and it relights, or rekindles! That means oxygen. Oxygen is made in photosynthesis, and when hydrogen peroxide breaks down into oxygen and water.
When magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid, the magnesium ribbon slowly gets smaller and seems to disappear. Where does it go?
The magnesium atoms didn't stop existing! They became part of a product, magnesium chloride. The acid supplied the chlorine atoms, and hydrogen gas bubbled away.
Reactants being used up is evidence of a chemical reaction. The atoms are simply rearranged into new substances.
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Is cooking an egg a physical or a chemical change? Pause the video now.
Answer: Chemical – new substances form and it can't be reversed.
Question 2: In the word equation iron + sulfur → iron sulfide, name the product. Pause the video now.
Answer: Iron sulfide.
Question 3: Chalk fizzes in vinegar and the mixture gets lighter. Have atoms been destroyed? Pause the video now.
Answer: No – carbon dioxide gas escapes; mass is conserved.
Question 4: Which gas relights a glowing splint? Pause the video now.
Answer: Oxygen.
